name: Question 5
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068221/assets/e15621dd6402a86de5c5d172880c7cbdc2a933e852259ad81d5ebcf9a89b9984.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}2x\,dA,\,$
where $D$ is the region enclosed between the curves ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=10$ and $y=2x+1,$ above the line $y=1,$ as shown in the picture.
worked_solution:
Notice that $D$ is a type II region. Since $x\ge 0,$ we obtain the following equations in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=10 & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}} \\ y=2x+1 & \,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}(y-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1) \\ 2\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}} & =y-1 \\ (2\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}})^{2} & =(y-1)^{2} \\ 40-4{y}^{2} & ={y}^{2}-2y+1 \\ 5{y}^{2}-2y-39 & =0 \\ (5y+13)(y-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=1$, the $y$-limits are 
$1\le y\le 3.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14068221/assets/33487fff6ff0b0e74bab4e6d6acdcb6902d40e938525d7de92d684ed5d98273a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,\frac{1}{2}(y-1)\le x\le \sqrt{10-{y}^{2}}}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}2x\,dA={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{(y-1)/2}^{\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}}}2x\,dx\,dy
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{(y-1)/2}^{\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}}}2x\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}[{\int }_{(y-1)/2}^{\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}}}2x\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}[{x}^{2}]_{(y-1)/2}^{\sqrt{10-{y}^{2}}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(10-{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(y-1)^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(10-{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(y-1)^{2})dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(10-{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(y-1)^{2})dy & ={[10y-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{12}(y-1)^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(30-9-\frac{2}{3})-(10-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{61}{3}-\frac{29}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that D is a type II region. Since x≥0, we obtain the following equations in terms of y:

x2+y2=10⟹x=10−y2y=2x+1⟹x=12(y−1)

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: 10−y2=12(y−1)210−y2=y−1(210−y2)2=(y−1)240−4y2=y2−2y+15y2−2y−39=0(5y+13)(y−3)=0 So, since our region lies above the line y=1, the y-limits are 1≤y≤3.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):1≤y≤3,12(y−1)≤x≤10−y2}.

So, we can express the integral as follows:

∬D2xdA=∫13∫(y−1)/210−y22xdxdy

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to x, treating y as a constant:

∫13∫(y−1)/210−y22xdxdy=∫13[∫(y−1)/210−y22xdx]dy=∫13[x2](y−1)/210−y2dy=∫13(10−y2−14(y−1)2)dy=∫13(10−y2−14(y−1)2)dy

Then, we integrate with respect to y:

∫13(10−y2−14(y−1)2)dy=[10y−13y3−112(y−1)3]13=(30−9−23)−(10−13)=613−293=323
